newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden seen fudging EMU membership decision.
newsitem.headline: Sweden seen fudging EMU membership decision.

text.p: Sweden is expected to fudge its long-awaited decision on joining Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) when it gives its view on Tuesday, economists said.

They were expecting Eurosceptic Sweden to give a qualified No to EMU membership, ruling out participation from the start in January 1999 but leaving the door open for later membership if strong public opposition to Swedish membership wanes.

Prime Minister Goran Persson has already warned that his minority Social Democratic government, whose support has slumped this year, would not give a simple yes or no answer -- but that the view would command a majority in parliament.
"I would view it as a fudge," PaineWebber economist James McKay told Reuters.
"Clearly the more complex the statement, then the more get-out clauses there will be for different scenarios."
He said the Socialist victory in France's weekend election was unlikely to boost the chances of a broader EMU membership and even increased the chances of a delayed EMU start.

But economists said uncertainty caused by France had no impact on the Swedish decision, to be taken by the Social Democrats' executive committee, the VU, ahead of party meetings later in June and the annual party congress in September.
JP Morgan economist Katharine Hoyland said the Swedish government needed to overcome continuing public opposition to EMU before making any commitment.

A poll by Skop last week found 30 percent of Swedes gave a flat 'no' to EMU membership when questioned in April and May compared to 27 percent polled in February, while 35 percent said Sweden should wait a few years, the same as the previous poll.

With Persson facing an election in September 1998, he would not be prepared to further jeopardise his party's popularity, which has slumped to 26.5 percent this year, its lowest since April 1991 and 18.5 percentage points below the 1994 election.
"While key figures in the government appear relatively in favour of the project, it tends to be the view of the public that is the main reason for holding back," said Hoyland.
Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, has come out in favour of joining EMU from the planned start in 1999.

But economist Julian Callow from Dresdner Kleinwort Benson said, "There are concerns the (Swedish) economy is much more cyclical than other European economies and it would be unwise to join EMU from the start when EMU is an unknown quantity. It is very unlikely that Sweden will be in at the start and the issue will become a specific election mandate."
Economists were not expecting major market reaction to Tuesday's statement.
"The markets are much more bothered about France," Callow said. "The markets have been forewarned in Sweden."

A radio report last week said Persson and Finance Minister Erik Asbrink had agreed the government could not join EMU during the current parliamentary term and that a general election would have to be held for Sweden to join EMU.
This meant Swedish EMU membership would probably be delayed beyond the next general election after EMU, in 2002.
"That report is typical in Sweden of leaking information to see how it is digested by the market," McKay said.
"I think most information has now been factored into the markets but if a very long delay is suggested or the decision is very anti-EMU then it could destabilise the market short-term."
